newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil's selloff of CVRD delayed, but not forever.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil's selloff of CVRD delayed, but not forever.

text.p: A Brazilian judge delayed Latin America's largest sale of state-owned assets Wednesday but the government vowed it would not give up on auctioning off the giant mining company CVRD.

Justice Democrito Ramos Reinaldo of the Superior Court of Justice, Brazil's highest court for non-constitutional matters, gave the government 10 days to come up with more information to back its appeal against rulings blocking the sale.
Asked if this meant the privatization, originally due to kick off on Tuesday, was off, a court spokesman said, "Yes".
On Tuesday, violent clashes between police and leftist demonstrators turned downtown Rio de Janeiro near the stock exchange into a battleground.

But on Wednesday the war in the courts took center stage. Justice Reinaldo had been mulling a government appeal to overrule 21 injunctions issued against the sale of Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), the world's largest iron ore producer and exporter.

The government argued that a "conflict of interpretation" meant all lawsuits should be judged by a single tribunal. Even as the country waited for Reinaldo's ruling, officials vowed the sale would eventually take place.
"We are going to continue making progress (towards selling CVRD) calmly and patiently," President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said in Brasilia. "We are not going to give up."

Seen as a key test of Cardoso's commitment to reforming the Brazilian economy, the sale of CVRD, which is also Latin America's biggest gold producer, could net the government about $5 billion, if completed.
Forty-five percent of CVRD's voting shares were supposed to have been sold on Tuesday.
Brazil's Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said later the sale would be rescheduled for May 2.
But Kandir denied the government had been dealt a severe blow by the delay.

"This is not a defeat. We always knew we would have to fight this one in the courts," Kandir told Globo television Wednesday morning when it began to become clear his lawyers were having a harder time than had been expected killing the lower court injunctions.

Experts said the flood of lawsuits -- 120 in all -- was partly due to a spat between Cardoso and the legal community, which has come under attack for privileges and high salaries. The CVRD privatization has mobilized considerable opposition from nationalists and leftists alike.
Opponents, ranging from former Presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco to Brazil's Catholic bishops, have accused the government of selling the country's mineral wealth to foreigners for a pittance.
The company enjoys a rare public sector reputation for efficiency and is Brazil's largest exporter, accounting for 5 percent of overseas sales.
Its Carajas mine, deep in the Amazon rain forest, holds the world's largest iron ore deposit estimated at 18 billion metric tons.
Two groups are ready to bid in the sale: one led by Brazilian steelmaker CSN, the other by local metal, cement and pulp producer Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
Australia's WMC Ltd was part of another consortium which was expected to bid for CVRD.
